entries.short: Two or more files with the same content.
entries.body: A duplicate is a file whose content matches another file exactly, byte for byte. Keeping one copy and removing the others frees space without losing anything.

entries.short: Files that are very similar but not identical — usually images.
entries.body: A near-duplicate looks the same to a person but differs in the actual bytes, for example a photo that was resized, cropped, or re-saved. DedupeDash finds these for images using a perceptual hash.

entries.short: Identical file content, confirmed by hashing.
entries.body: An exact match means the files are the same byte for byte. DedupeDash confirms it with a size check, a SHA-256 hash, and an optional byte-for-byte comparison.

entries.short: Whether files are identical (Exact) or just look alike (Images).
entries.body: Exact groups contain files with the same content. Image groups contain pictures that look alike but are not identical — review those visually before removing them.

entries.short: A fingerprint of what an image looks like, not its exact bytes.
entries.body: A perceptual hash turns an image into a short fingerprint based on its appearance, so two pictures that look the same get similar fingerprints even after resizing or re-saving.

entries.short: How many bits two image fingerprints differ by — lower means more alike.
entries.body: The distance counts how many bits differ between two image fingerprints. 0 means they look identical; a small number means very similar. A lower threshold is stricter.

entries.short: The number of differing bits between two fingerprints.
entries.body: The Hamming distance is how many positions differ between two equal-length fingerprints. DedupeDash groups images whose perceptual hashes are within a chosen distance.

entries.short: A secure fingerprint of a file's exact content.
entries.body: SHA-256 produces a fixed-length fingerprint of a file. Two files with the same SHA-256 have the same content; DedupeDash uses it to confirm exact duplicates.

entries.short: Comparing every byte to be completely sure files match.
entries.body: A byte-for-byte comparison reads both files fully and checks every byte. It is the final safety step that rules out the rare chance of a hash coincidence before anything is removed.

entries.short: Adds a reference hard-link (after deleting the duplicate) that allows for any other processes (referencing the deleted file) to instead reference the remaining file.
entries.body: A hard link makes two file names point at the exact same data on disk. When you hard-link a duplicate, the duplicate is deleted and replaced with a link to the file you keep — so the freed copy no longer takes up space, yet its path still works and opens the same content. That is the nice part: any app, script, or system operation that relied on the duplicate's location keeps working, because the link is indistinguishable from the original file. The data is stored a single time, so you reclaim the space without losing any path. Both files must be on the same drive (filesystem); across drives, use Move to Trash instead. If you later edit through one path, the change is seen through the other, because they are literally the same file.

entries.short: Leaves these files exactly as they are and skips them in all future scans — no copy is removed or changed.
entries.body: Ignoring a group takes no action on the files now and adds them to a skip list, so later scans will not flag them again. Use it for copies you intend to keep on purpose (for example, deliberate duplicates in different folders). You can clear the ignore list from Settings to have them considered again.

entries.short: A shortcut that points to another file by its path.
entries.body: A symbolic link is a small file that points to another path. Unlike a hard link, it breaks if the target moves or is deleted.

entries.short: A copy-on-write clone that shares storage until one side changes.
entries.body: On filesystems that support it (such as Btrfs), a reflink shares the data of two files until one is modified, giving the space savings of a link with the independence of a copy.

entries.short: Removes a file to the Trash, where it can be restored.
entries.body: Moving to Trash puts the file in your desktop's Trash folder. Nothing is permanently gone — you can restore it from your file manager until you empty the Trash.

entries.short: The one file in a group DedupeDash suggests you keep.
entries.body: The keeper is the best copy in a duplicate group by the keep policy — for images the highest resolution, for backups the newest. The other files in the group are the removal candidates.

entries.short: How much room you would free by removing the extra copies.
entries.body: Reclaimable space is the total size of the non-keeper files in a group or scan — what you get back if you remove or hard-link the extras.

entries.short: A preview of what would be removed, with nothing actually changed.
entries.body: A dry-run shows exactly which files would be removed so you can review before committing. DedupeDash never changes anything until you confirm.

entries.short: A large side-by-side view to confirm files really are duplicates.
entries.body: SpotCheck opens a duplicate group and shows each file at a readable size — full image previews or document snippets — so you can confirm the copies match before removing them.

entries.short: An A/B comparison that makes small changes between images obvious.
entries.body: The difference view compares the keeper with a candidate so a crop, watermark, or re-compression stands out. Use it when two images look almost the same.

entries.short: An older saved copy of a file you still have a newer version of.
entries.body: A backup is a copy kept for safety, often named with ~, .bak, .old, a date, or the word 'backup'. When a file is flagged as a probable backup, DedupeDash suggests keeping the newest copy and removing the older ones.

entries.short: Which backup is the most recent (kept) and which are older (candidates).
entries.body: Within a backup group, the most recent file is marked Newest and kept by default; the rest are marked Older with how much older they are, so you can remove stale backups and keep the current one.

entries.short: A file owned by the operating system, not your content.
entries.body: System files live in places like /usr, /proc, and /boot and are managed by the OS. DedupeDash skips them by default because they are not your data and should not be removed.

entries.short: Temporary files apps recreate on demand.
entries.body: A cache holds temporary data an application can rebuild automatically, such as thumbnails or browser data. Skipping caches keeps the scan focused on files that matter.

entries.short: A small preview image the system generates automatically.
entries.body: Thumbnails are small previews your desktop creates for images and videos. They are regenerated as needed, so they are not worth deduplicating.

entries.short: Files a package manager or build creates and can recreate.
entries.body: Folders like node_modules, __pycache__, and build output are produced by tools and can be regenerated at any time, so DedupeDash can skip them.

entries.short: Folders and files the scan skips because they are safe to ignore.
entries.body: Exclusion presets skip system files, caches, build artifacts, and other things an app or the OS can recreate. Excluded paths are never scanned and can never be removed.

entries.short: Simple finds exact and image duplicates; Advanced adds more signals.
entries.body: Simple Scan covers what most people need: exact duplicates and image near-duplicates with sensible defaults. Advanced Scan adds extra matching signals and finer control.

entries.short: Skip files smaller than this size.
entries.body: Setting a minimum size skips very small files, which are rarely worth deduplicating and can clutter results.

entries.term: Will this delete my only copy?
entries.short: No — DedupeDash always keeps one file in every group.
entries.body: Every duplicate group keeps exactly one file (the keeper). Only the extra copies are ever offered for removal, and removals go to Trash by default so they can be restored.

entries.short: The copies are replaced by links to the keeper and share its storage.
entries.body: Hard-linking keeps every path working but stores the data once, so you reclaim the space without losing any location. It works within a single drive.

entries.short: No — backups are only flagged; you decide what to remove.
entries.body: DedupeDash marks probable backups and suggests keeping the newest, but it never removes anything on its own. You review and confirm every action.
